The claim states that the method 'differs from standard color blending by operating on intermediate feature maps rather than raw colors'. While the evidence confirms that the method operates on 'intermediate feature maps' (specifically 'aggregated pixel alignment feature Fp' derived from image features fqk) and uses these to predict color, it does not explicitly state that this is a difference from 'standard color blending' nor does it characterize standard color blending as operating on 'raw colors'. The evidence describes the mechanism (feature aggregation and MLP weighting) but does not provide the comparative context or the specific definition of 'standard color blending' required to support the claim's assertion of difference.

See [HumanNeRF](https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.00759) [S2].

The claim accurately reflects the details provided in Source [S2]. The source explicitly states that the method aggregates pixel alignment features from multiple source views using viewing directions and angles relative to source views. It confirms the projection of spatial point p into view k to fetch feature vector fqk, the computation of the aggregated feature Fp as a weighted summation, and the estimation of blending weights wk via an MLP network using view direction v, angle theta, and feature fqk.

HumanNeRF introduced feature blending for dynamic human radiance fields from sparse inputs [S2].

The evidence explicitly describes a method for dynamic human radiance fields that involves projecting points into multiple source views, fetching features, and computing an aggregated feature Fp via a weighted summation (blending) of these features. The weights are estimated by an MLP. This matches the claim's description of 'feature blending for dynamic human radiance fields'. The context of using SMPL and handling dynamics confirms the 'dynamic human' aspect. While the specific name 'HumanNeRF' is not in the provided text snippet, the technical description of the mechanism (feature blending from sparse/multiple views for dynamic humans) is fully supported by the evidence.

Multi-View Color Blending fuses original colors from $N$ reference views into query points using view-dependent weights derived from feature similarity and view direction [S1, S2].

The claim states that Multi-View Color Blending fuses original colors from N reference views into query points using view-dependent weights derived from feature similarity and view direction. Source [S1] explicitly states that it 'utilize[s] color blending to fuse original colors in different views to the query points' and defines the weights based on feature similarity (via feature concatenation and attention mechanisms implied in the context of feature extraction) and view direction (via the dot product of view directions). Source [S2] corroborates this by describing the aggregation of features from multiple views using blending weights estimated by an MLP based on view direction and angles. Both sources confirm the mechanism described in the claim.
